System intent

01 / 13

Designed around the moments where healthcare software fails.

The system reduces ambiguity at handoffs, protects clinical decisions and keeps work recoverable when people, processes or technology are under pressure.

Patient contextPersistent
Safety signalsPrioritised
Role ownershipExplicit
System stateRecoverable

Safety is expressed through hierarchy, language, interaction and recovery—not through decorative red.

Ten design principles

A decision framework for every clinical interface.

These principles govern foundations, components, role-based workspaces and the integrated outpatient journey.

01

Identity before action

Patient, encounter, location and care context remain visible before any consequential action.

02

Safety earns interruption

Critical alerts interrupt the workflow only when immediate clinical attention is justified.

03

System state stays visible

Users can always understand whether information is saved, syncing, delayed, blocked or offline.

04

Roles have clear contracts

Each workspace reflects the decisions, permissions and responsibilities of its clinical role.

05

Workflow before screens

Components support complete care journeys and handoffs—not isolated pages or decorative dashboards.

06

Provenance is preserved

Clinical information shows its source, author, timestamp and status wherever trust depends on it.

07

Ownership is explicit

Tasks, exceptions and approvals clearly identify who must act, what is due and what happens next.

08

Recovery is designed

Interrupted work can be safely resumed without duplicate actions, lost data or hidden system changes.

09

Access is operational

Keyboard use, readable contrast, safe target sizes and multilingual readiness are system requirements.

10

Variation is governed

Tokens, components and clinical rules create consistency while allowing controlled product evolution.

Accessibility · 05 / 13

Accessibility is part of the clinical safety model.

Hospital interfaces must remain understandable and operable across different abilities, devices, environments and levels of urgency.

Accessibility is verified inside complete workflows because clinical risk often appears through context, sequence and state.

Contrast, scale and target size are treated as operational requirements rather than final-stage visual adjustments.

Accessibility acceptance rule

Content and language · 06 / 13

Clinical language reduces hesitation at the point of care.

Interface content helps people understand the current situation, make a safe decision and know exactly what happens next.

Concision never removes essential clinical context, ownership or consequence.

Writing foundations

Every message supports one clear clinical decision.

01

Name the action

Use specific clinical verbs such as review, acknowledge, prescribe and sign.

02

Explain the reason

State why information or confirmation is required before asking for it.

03

Reveal the consequence

High-risk messages explain what could happen if the action is delayed.

04

Identify ownership

Make the responsible person, role or team explicit at every handoff.

Action-oriented microcopy

Replace generic instructions with explicit guidance.

Avoid

Something went wrong.

Please try again later.

Use

The medication order could not be saved.

Your entered information is preserved. Check the connection and save the order again.

Message anatomy

Risk messages answer four questions in sequence.

01

What happened

Potassium result is critical

02

Clinical context

Result: 6.7 mmol/L · Reference: 3.5–5.1

03

Consequence

Delay could result in cardiac complications.

04

Required action

Assess the patient and notify the responsible clinician.

Controlled terminology

Stable language makes actions predictable across workflows.

ProceedReview dose and continueExplains what must happen next.

Localization rules

Meaning remains stable across languages.

  • Preserve medication names, units and reference ranges.
  • Use familiar local terms without changing clinical meaning.
  • Allow longer translated text without truncating actions.
  • Validate high-risk translations with clinical reviewers.

Clinical content rule

Every message explains the situation, preserves essential context, identifies ownership and provides a specific next action.

HOS-CONTENT-001 · CLINICALLY REVIEWED

Hospital information is organized around roles, patients, encounters and clinical tasks instead of disconnected software modules.

People should always understand where they are, whose information they are viewing and what action comes next.

External referral · 08 / 13

Referrals remain accountable beyond the hospital boundary.

The referral service coordinates clinical information, consent, authorization, secure exchange and follow-up when care moves to an external organization.

Sending documents is not completion. The loop closes only when the receiving provider acknowledges responsibility and returns the outcome.

Referral workflow

One traceable journey from clinical need to continuity of care.

  1. Identify

    Confirm the clinical need for external care.

  2. Prepare

    Assemble the minimum referral package.

  3. 03Current

    Authorize

    Verify consent and financial approval.

  4. 04

    Send

    Transfer the referral through a secure channel.

  5. 05

    Confirm

    Receive acknowledgement from the provider.

  6. 06

    Close loop

    Reconcile the outcome into the patient record.

A referral is complete only when consent, authorization, secure exchange, receiving-provider acknowledgement and returned clinical outcomes are traceable in the patient record.

Role-based workspaces · 09 / 13

Each role sees the same hospital through a different responsibility.

Workspaces prioritize the patients, tasks, decisions and exceptions relevant to the current role while preserving one shared clinical record.

Role adaptation changes priority and available actions. It never changes the meaning of clinical information.

Workspace contract

Adaptation never removes safety or accountability.

Role before menu

The workspace begins with the responsibilities of the signed-in role instead of exposing every module.

Patient context persists

Identity, encounter, allergies, location and care team remain visible while tasks change.

Ownership is explicit

Every task identifies who owns it, when it is due and what completes it.

Permissions explain recovery

Restricted actions preserve prepared work and show the correct approval path.

System states & recovery · 10 / 13

Every system response must explain what happened and what happens next.

Hospital work cannot disappear behind generic spinners, silent failures or disabled controls. Every state preserves context, communicates impact and supports safe recovery.

State severity follows clinical consequence—not visual decoration or technical implementation.

Semantic state families

Color, language and interruption level communicate one meaning.

Informational

Explain context without interrupting work.

Example

Referral package updated 4 minutes ago.

In progress

Show active processing and expected completion.

Example

Insurance authorization is being reviewed.

Successful

Confirm completion and preserve evidence.

Example

Clinical note signed and added to the record.

Warning

Expose risk while safe continuation remains possible.

Example

Authorization expires within 24 hours.

Critical

Interrupt when clinical or operational harm is possible.

Example

Potassium result requires acknowledgement.

Restricted

Explain why an action is unavailable and who can help.

Example

Clinical approval is required before cancellation.

Recovery contract

Recovery follows one predictable four-step structure.

  1. 01

    Preserve

    Keep valid entries, selections, filters and patient context intact.

  2. 02

    Explain

    State what happened, what was affected and whether clinical work is safe.

  3. 03

    Route

    Identify the person, permission or system responsible for resolution.

  4. 04

    Recover

    Provide a safe retry, alternate workflow or clearly monitored queue.

Empty-state distinctions

An empty surface must explain whether work is absent, complete or restricted.

No results

No patients match “Meera Nair” within Cardiology OPD today.

Work queue complete

All assigned critical-result acknowledgements have been completed.

Access restricted

Medication pricing is available only to authorized billing roles.

Critical states require acknowledgement

Clinical risk remains active until a named owner reviews the event, records the response and completes the acknowledgement.

Never dismiss automatically

Disabled actions require an explanation

The interface identifies the unmet condition, preserves prepared work and shows the role or approval needed to continue.

Never rely on reduced opacity alone

System-state rule

Every state communicates cause, impact, ownership, persistence and the safest next action. Failure never removes patient context or silently discards completed work.

HOS-STATE-001 · RECOVERY VERIFIED

Privacy, access & audit · 11 / 13

Sensitive access must remain purposeful, limited and accountable.

Hospital access is determined by identity, role, care relationship, declared purpose and clinical consequence—not role labels alone.

Restricted information stays discoverable as a protected placeholder so users understand what exists and how to request it.

Access decision model

Permission is evaluated for every sensitive action.

  1. 01

    Identity

    Confirm the authenticated person and active professional role.

  2. 02

    Relationship

    Verify an active care, operational or administrative relationship.

  3. 03

    Purpose

    Match the requested information to a valid work purpose.

  4. 04

    Scope

    Reveal only the minimum information required for the task.

  5. 05

    Evidence

    Record access, decisions, exports and exceptional disclosure.

Restricted-record pattern

Protection does not create a misleading empty record.

Privacy patterns

Privacy remains visible through behavior, not policy text alone.

Restricted record

Preserve the existence of the record while masking content the current role cannot access.

Explain restriction and escalation path

Privacy veil

Temporarily conceal patient details when the workspace is unattended or externally visible.

Restore only after identity verification

Minimum necessary

Display only the patient, financial or clinical information needed for the active responsibility.

Scope follows role and purpose

Controlled disclosure

Printing and exporting require a declared purpose, appropriate permission and traceable evidence.

Every disclosure remains auditable

Privacy veil protects unattended workspaces

Patient details are concealed after inactivity, manual activation or display-sharing detection. Unsaved work remains protected underneath the veil.

HOS-PRIV-001 · ACCESS VERIFIED

Governance & contribution · 12 / 13

Safe consistency requires ownership, evidence and controlled change.

Core components are centrally governed while specialties and encounters extend them through a reviewed contribution model.

Every accepted change includes accessibility, state, audit, localization, versioning and migration evidence.

Contribution lifecycle

Contributions move through one visible, evidence-based path.

  1. 01

    Define the problem

    Describe the user, workflow, risk and evidence behind the requested change.

  2. 02

    Review the gap

    Confirm that an existing component, variant or composition cannot solve it safely.

  3. 03

    Assign reviewers

    Identify the design, clinical, accessibility, privacy and engineering owners required.

  4. 04

    Specify behavior

    Document anatomy, permissions, content, states, provenance and recovery.

  5. 05

    Verify evidence

    Test usability, keyboard behavior, assistive technology and safety-critical paths.

  6. 06

    Release responsibly

    Version the change, publish guidance and provide migration support.

Definition of ready

Design begins only after the problem and risk are understood.

  • Clear user and workflow problem
  • Existing-component gap analysis
  • Permission and privacy model
  • Required data and provenance
  • Required interaction and system states
  • Keyboard and screen-reader behavior
  • Offline and error behavior where relevant
  • Analytics and audit requirements where relevant

Definition of done

Completion requires verified behavior—not a polished default state.

  • Visual and interaction specification complete
  • Token use documented with no arbitrary values
  • WCAG 2.2 AA review complete
  • 200% zoom and text-spacing review complete
  • Keyboard path verified
  • Error, empty, loading, restricted and offline states covered
  • English expansion and one Indian-script sample checked
  • Critical and irreversible workflows reviewed separately

Deprecation contract

Removal follows a controlled and traceable migration.

  1. 01

    Mark the pattern

    Show that the component is deprecated and explain why.

  2. 02

    Name the replacement

    Provide the supported alternative and migration examples.

  3. 03

    Track remaining use

    Identify products, templates and records still depending on it.

  4. 04

    Preserve history

    Maintain rendering required for signed or exported records.

  5. 05

    Remove after review

    Complete the migration window and final risk assessment.

Template governance

Governed clinical content cannot be silently changed.

Named owner

Every template has an accountable clinical owner.

Version and scope

The effective version and supported encounter are visible.

Controlled rollout

Updates use versioned release and migration rules.

Historical integrity

Signed records retain the template version used.

Personal shortcuts remain separate from governed content

A clinician may create personal convenience text, but it cannot silently alter required fields, safety instructions, consent language or the approved clinical template.

Clinical change is never treated as cosmetic

A wording, color, timing or interaction change can alter clinical interpretation and must receive review proportional to its risk.

Consequence determines review depth

Version evidence travels with the product

Components, templates and historical records retain the version needed to explain behavior, reproduce evidence and support safe migration.

Never overwrite historical meaning

Governance rule

Every contribution begins with a demonstrated workflow problem, names accountable reviewers, specifies all consequential states and releases with evidence, versioning and a safe migration path.

HOS-GOV-001 · CHANGE CONTROLLED

Release & migration roadmap · 13 / 13

Release the system through proven journeys—not a simultaneous visual rewrite.

Hospital OS begins with shared foundations, proves them through outpatient care, strengthens exceptional behavior and then scales across specialties and facilities.

Each release must remain independently adoptable, reversible, measurable and safe for historical clinical evidence.

Controlled release sequence

Capability expands only after the previous safety contract is proven.

  1. Release 01

    Weeks 01–08

    Foundation

    Establish the shared language, safety context and accessible application structure.

    Exit gate

    Foundation verified before product migration begins

  2. Release 02

    Weeks 09–18

    OPD core

    Validate the system through a complete outpatient journey involving multiple roles.

    Exit gate

    One complete clinical journey works across roles

  3. Release 03

    Weeks 19–28

    Safety & resilience

    Add the exceptional, degraded and high-consequence behavior required for clinical trust.

    Exit gate

    Exceptional paths remain safe and recoverable

  4. Release 04

    Week 29 onward

    Scale

    Extend validated foundations across specialties, facilities and governed automation.

    Exit gate

    Expansion reuses the shared contract without weakening it

Migration path

Migration is a clinical change programme—not a component replacement exercise.

  1. 01

    Inventory current patterns

    Identify screens, components, templates, arbitrary values and duplicate behavior.

    Owner · Product and design

    Evidence · Current-state inventory

  2. 02

    Map to shared foundations

    Translate legacy colors, typography, spacing, statuses and controls into semantic tokens.

    Owner · Design-system team

    Evidence · Token mapping record

  3. 03

    Classify workflow risk

    Prioritize patient identity, medication, critical-result and irreversible workflows.

    Owner · Clinical governance

    Evidence · Risk classification

  4. 04

    Pilot one complete journey

    Migrate an end-to-end workflow instead of validating isolated polished screens.

    Owner · Pilot product team

    Evidence · Usability and safety findings

  5. 05

    Prepare people and operations

    Publish guidance, train affected roles and prepare support and escalation paths.

    Owner · Operations and enablement

    Evidence · Readiness record

  6. 06

    Release with rollback

    Deploy in controlled stages with monitoring, recovery ownership and a rollback condition.

    Owner · Engineering and operations

    Evidence · Release decision log

  7. 07

    Measure real adoption

    Track supported-component use, task outcomes, defects and safety guardrails.

    Owner · System owner

    Evidence · Adoption dashboard

  8. 08

    Retire legacy behavior

    Remove old patterns only after usage ends and historical evidence remains available.

    Owner · Product maintainers

    Evidence · Deprecation closure

Decision model

Continue, contain or roll back using predefined evidence.

Continue

Outcomes meet thresholds and no unresolved safety condition exists.

Contain

Limit the cohort while a bounded defect or support issue is corrected.

Roll back

Restore the verified prior path when safety or record integrity is uncertain.

Schedule pressure never overrides a safety, privacy, accessibility or historical-integrity gate.
